designs.name: ngs-screen
designs.description: Run the Sanchez-Rivera lab sensor screen NGS pipeline end to end — paired-end FASTQ to per-guide counts, to per-guide CRISPResso2 editing rates, to lane- and replicate-merged editing tables and a MAGeCK-ready count matrix. Covers both the base-editing layout (15 nt Hamming_BC + 42 nt sensor, --base_editor_output, quantification window 6-35) and the prime-editing extended-barcode layout (16 nt matching BC overlapping the sensor by 8 nt, 55 nt sensor, --prime_editor_output, per-pegRNA wt_qwc/edit_qwc). Writes the STEP3 config file from a sequencing run folder, validates the library CSV columns (gRNA_id or pegRNA_id, Protospacer, Hamming_BC, sensor_wt, sensor_alt) and the bc_len/sensor_len implied by them, generates the SLURM array sbatch scripts for Luria with the right --array range and micromamba env, then locally compiles crispresso aggregated CSVs into tidy editing tables and builds the count matrix. Use whenever asked to process sensor screen NGS data, make a config file for a sequencing run, set up or edit the STEP4/5/6 cluster scripts, "run CRISPResso on the sensors", compile or aggregate CRISPResso output, merge NGS lanes or biological replicates, compute sensor editing percentages (corr_perc, target_base_edit_perc, byproduct rates), build a guide count matrix or MAGeCK input, or debug low read-assignment / high recombination / "no_match_bc" rates in a screen. Does NOT compute LFC, empirical p-values or FDR — that is the screen-stats skill.
designs.whenToUse: Fires for anything between raw paired-end sensor-screen FASTQs and the two tidy outputs (per-guide editing tables, per-guide count matrix); it does not fire for library design upstream (library-design), for LFC/empirical-FDR/hit-calling downstream (screen-stats), or for arrayed single-locus amplicon genotyping (genotyping).
coreCapabilities: Write the STEP3 config file (space-separated ArrayTaskID R1_FILE R2_FILE folder_name, numbered from 1) by scanning a sequencing run folder for per-sample subdirectories and sorting the two *_1_sequence.fastq / *_2_sequence.fastq per sample, replacing the notebook's brittle `k[:3]=='D25'` prefix filter and its `if len(j)==2 ... else j[2],j[3]` hack with a regex on _1_/_2_.
designs.inputs: Two things the user supplies. (1) A sequencing run folder on the cluster or mounted at /Volumes/sanchezrivera/<user>/<run>, containing one subfolder per NGS sample with uncompressed paired FASTQs named *_1_sequence.fastq (R1 = sensor read) and *_2_sequence.fastq (R2 = protospacer read); GZ=False is hardcoded in every extraction script, so .fastq.gz must be gunzipped first. (2) A library CSV with exact column names: gRNA_id (BE) or pegRNA_id (PE), Protospacer (21 nt including the leading G — the scripts use [1:] to get the 19 nt matched against R2), Hamming_BC (given in the library as the sense-strand barcode; the script reverse-complements it to match R1), sensor_wt and sensor_alt (the two CRISPResso amplicons, --amplicon_seq and --expected_hdr_amplicon_seq). For PE additionally wt_qwc and edit_qwc (per-pegRNA quantification-window coordinate strings). For the count matrix additionally gene_name_m, classification (values 'non-targeting control' / 'safe-targeting control' get collapsed to the single gene name controlsgRNA) and Editor ('ABE'/'CBE') for subpool filtering. bc_len and sensor_len are not free parameters — they must equal len(Hamming_BC) and len(sensor_wt) and the skill checks this.
designs.outputs: On the cluster, four folders that must pre-exist in the run directory with exactly these lowercase names or STEP4/5/6 crash: counts/ (<folder_name>_count_df.csv with Guide_ID, sgRNA_no_Gstart, unique_BC, total_guide_count, matched_guide_count, bc_count, duplicate_sgRNA), classification/ (<folder_name>_classification_df.csv with the 10 outcome rows good quality / low_qual_r1 / low_qual_r2 / low_qual_r12 / no_match_bc / bc_identified / proto_identified_perfect / proto_identified_imperfect / proto_identified_recombined / no_match_proto), confusion_mats/ (protospacer x barcode recombination matrix), and crispresso/<folder_name>/CRISPResso_on_<guide_id>/ plus crispresso/<folder_name>_crispresso_aggregated.csv. Locally: per-sample tidy editing tables with Guide_ID, Reads_in_input, Reads_lowqual, Reads_aligned_all_amplicons, Reads_aligned_WT, Reads_aligned_HDR, Reads_unaligned, WT, correct_edit, target_base_edit, byproduct_all, byproduct_INDEL, byproduct_sub, byproduct_ambiguous plus the seven _perc columns (corr_perc, target_base_edit_perc, WT_perc, byproduct_all_perc, byproduct_INDEL_perc, byproduct_sub_perc, byproduct_ambiguous_perc); lane-merged copies as <sample>_compact_unfiltered.csv; replicate-merged MLE tables as <condition>.csv (the exact files screen-stats' attach_editing_info reads); and a tab-separated MAGeCK-ready count matrix with columns sgRNA, gene, then one column per biological sample.

gotchas: REAL BUG, silently ignores your setting: sensor_extraction_42nt_trimming_quality.py line 246 calls `quality_checker(q1,q2)` with only two arguments, although the function signature is `quality_checker(q1, q2, bc_len, sensor_len, proto_len=19, mode='region_average', ...)`. bc_len and sensor_len are missing positional args — this is a TypeError, so the script crashes immediately; if anyone 'fixed' it by giving those params defaults, the quality_check_mode passed as argv[8] from the .sh is still never used and every run silently falls back to region_average. The PE sibling at line 246 does it correctly (`quality_checker(q1, q2, bc_len, sensor_len, mode=quality_check_mode)`). The skill's engine must pass all four.

REAL BUG, corrupts PE sensor extraction: in sensor_extraction_peg_counts_ext_bc_16nt.py, `to_IOSeq_rec(sensor_seq, i, q1, real_bc_len, sensor_len)` slices `sensor_seq[real_bc_len:real_bc_len+sensor_len]`, but all three call sites (lines 275, 294, 336) pass `bc_len` (16) instead of `real_bc_len` (8). Every extracted PE sensor therefore starts 8 nt downstream of where it should and ends 8 nt past the intended window, so the per-guide fastq reads no longer align to the 55 nt sensor_wt amplicon and CRISPResso reports collapsed or zero alignment. Must pass real_bc_len.

REAL BUG, mislabels samples: in counts.ipynb's count_matrix, `new_sample_ids = np.unique([x.rsplit('-',1)[0] for x in samp_id])` is alphabetically sorted, while `samps_to_merge` is built in config/file order. The loop then does `join_out[new_sample_ids[i]] = join_out[samps_to_merge[i]].sum(axis=1)`, pairing the i-th lane pair with the i-th alphabetical name. With names like lib, input, d5, d15-rep1..5, spleen1..5, bm1..5, men1..5 the orders differ, so counts get written under the wrong sample column. STEP7's merge_NGS_replicates does it right with `dict.fromkeys`; use that.

bc_len and sensor_len in the .sh are not parameters you tune — they must equal len(Hamming_BC) and len(sensor_wt) in the library. The BE default pair is 15/42; the PE extended-BC layout is the exception, where bc_len=16 is the matching length (8 nt real barcode + first 8 nt of sensor) while real_bc_len=8 is where the sensor actually starts, and sensor_len=55.

GZ=False is hardcoded as a module global in every extraction script and is not exposed on the command line. Compressed FASTQs will be read as text and produce zero matches with no error. Gunzip first, or flip GZ.

The four output folders counts/, classification/, confusion_mats/, crispresso/ must be created by hand in the run directory, lowercase and exactly spelled, before STEP4 — the scripts write straight to 'counts/' + ... with no makedirs and the array task dies on the final to_csv after all the compute is done.

extraction_filtration starts with `os.mkdir(folder_name)` and will raise FileExistsError if the folder already exists, so re-running a failed array task requires deleting the per-sample folder first. Re-running also matters because the per-guide fastqs are opened in append mode ('a'), so a partial rerun into an existing folder would double-count reads.

The library's Hamming_BC is reverse-complemented by the script (`bc_list = [str(Bio.Seq.Seq(i).reverse_complement()) for i in input_df['Hamming_BC']]`) before matching R1. If your library file already stores the R1-strand barcode, every read lands in no_match_bc and counts come back all zero. Check the no_match_bc fraction in classification/ on the first sample before launching the full array.

Protospacer is expected to be 21 nt with a leading G; the scripts take `val['Protospacer'][1:]` for the 19 nt compared against `r2[:19]` and for CRISPResso's --guide_seq. A library that stores the 20 nt protospacer without the G start will be silently off by one base at both ends.

The three count columns mean different things and are not interchangeable: matched_guide_count (barcode and protospacer both correct — stringent), bc_count (barcode correct regardless of protospacer, includes recombinants — highest), total_guide_count (protospacer correct regardless of barcode, also incremented for recombined reads). bc_count is the notebook default. Pick one and keep it fixed across a paper; recombination rate determines how far apart they are.

For a duplicated protospacer in the library (duplicate_sgRNA=True), `df1.loc[df1['sgRNA_no_Gstart']==proto, 'total_guide_count']+=1` increments every row sharing that protospacer, so total_guide_count is inflated for duplicates. bc_count and matched_guide_count are per-barcode and unaffected.

The recombination fallback loop in extraction_filtration is O(library size) per unmatched read and `df1.loc[df1['unique_BC']==bc, ...]` is a full boolean scan of the library per read; the inner `if count==len(proto_list)` test is also wrong when the break fires on the last element. On a multi-million-read FASTQ with a few thousand guides this is the pipeline's whole runtime.

STEP6 does `os.listdir(fp + '/' + sample_name + f'/CRISPResso_on_{guide_id}')` with no existence check — one guide whose CRISPResso run never produced a directory (not merely a missing quantification file) raises FileNotFoundError and the whole sample's aggregation is lost. The blank-row fallback only covers the case where the directory exists but the quantification txt does not.

crispresso_quant_blank.csv must be in the run directory alongside the aggregation script or STEP6 fails; its Reference and HDR rows of zeros are what makes a failed guide appear as 0 reads rather than vanish from the table. Ship it with the skill.

The BE quantification window is hardcoded as `--quantification_window_coordinates 6-35,6-35` — 5 nt flanks around a 20 nt protospacer inside a 42 nt sensor. Change the sensor design or its flank lengths and this window silently quantifies the wrong bases. PE instead reads per-row wt_qwc/edit_qwc from the library, so for PE the window lives in the library file.
`--base_editor_output` vs `--prime_editor_output` and `--plot_window_size 5` vs `15` are the other BE/PE differences; mixing them up changes how CRISPResso classifies substitutions.

In crispresso_compiler, correct_edit = HDR-amplicon Unmodified, target_base_edit = HDR Modified + HDR Unmodified, and byproduct_all folds the unaligned reads (Reads_aligned_all_amplicons - HDR aligned - WT aligned) into the byproduct bucket, with byproduct_ambiguous computed as the residual byproduct_all - sub_all - indel_all. All percentages are over Reads_aligned_all_amplicons, not Reads_in_input. byproduct_ambiguous can go negative on low-read guides; the function only does fillna(0), not clipping.

MLE_merge_auto sums raw counts then recomputes percentages, so a replicate with 10x the reads carries 10x the weight — this is intentional (maximum-likelihood merge), not a bug, but it means a single deep replicate can dominate a condition. It asserts Guide_ID order matches across replicates and will fail loudly if the subpool filters differed between samples. The legacy MLE_merge only handles exactly 3 replicates.

merge_NGS_replicates blindly pairs every two consecutive entries in sample_ids and strips the trailing -N. If any sample has one lane instead of two, the pairing shifts and merges reads from two different biological samples with no error. Verify every sample has exactly two lanes, or build the groups explicitly with MLE_merge_auto.

Subpool hygiene is the one thing the notebook shouts about: an ABE count matrix must be filtered to `df[df['Editor']=='ABE']['gRNA_id']` before MAGeCK or LFC analysis. Leaving CBE guides in an ABE file does not error — it just changes every column's depth normalization and quietly destroys the LFC.

Only guides whose classification is exactly 'non-targeting control' or 'safe-targeting control' get collapsed to the gene name controlsgRNA. Any other spelling in the library leaves controls as separate single-guide 'genes' and breaks both MAGeCK's negative-control handling and screen-stats' control-guide null.

STEP7 and STEP8 notebooks carry hardcoded absolute paths (/Users/kexindong/Documents/GitHub/PhD-FSR-MH-Lab/07_B-ALL_resubmission_20250819/..., '.../FINAL_focused_library.csv', '.../counts') and the STEP3 config notebook hardcodes /Volumes/sanchezrivera/kexindong/251030Hem plus a `k[:3]=='D25'` sample-prefix filter. None of these may survive into the skill — everything goes through CLI args, $LABROOT and $LAB_DATA_ROOT.

The shipped sbatch scripts contain `srun --pty bash` in the body. That is a copy-paste artifact from the interactive setup instructions; leaving it in a batch submission is wrong and the generated scripts must omit it. They also hardcode /net/bmc-lab2/data/lab/sanchezrivera/kexindong/251030Hem and kexindon@mit.edu or XXX@mit.edu as --mail-user.

--array=1-N must equal the number of config rows (188 in the shipped example). A wrong N either skips samples silently (too small) or produces tasks whose awk lookup returns an empty R1_FILE and crashes confusingly (too large).
CRISPResso can fail on group write permissions on the shared filesystem; the documented fix is `chmod -R g+w $LABROOT/<run>/crispresso`.

The PE layout exists because of unusually high barcode-protospacer recombination in earlier PE screens; the 8 nt extension into the sensor is a specificity fix. Read confusion_mats/ off-diagonal mass before trusting any PE counts, and expect the three count columns to diverge most there.

sensor_env.yml carries `name: sensor_lib_sg` and `prefix: /home/samgould/.conda/envs/sensor_lib_sg`, so `micromamba create -n sensor_env -f sensor_env.yml` creates something named inconsistently with every .sh that does `micromamba activate sensor_env`. Strip prefix and set name before creating.

Do not run STEP7/STEP8 inside the pegg environment. pegg needs Python 3.9/3.10 with scikit-learn==1.1.1 and numpy<2 because its pickled models break otherwise; that constraint belongs to library-design, and the compile/count-matrix code only needs pandas and numpy.
designs.runtimeCharacter: STEP4 is the bottleneck and dominates everything: a pure-Python per-read loop with a full-library boolean DataFrame scan per read plus an O(library) Hamming fallback per unmatched read, writing one fastq record at a time with an open/append per read. Budget tens of minutes to a few hours per sample on a multi-million-read FASTQ with a few thousand guides — but it is embarrassingly parallel, so as a SLURM array (--array=1-188 in the shipped example, 1 node / 1 core / sample) the wall clock is one sample, not 188. Memory is small, well under a few GB: only the library tables, the per-guide count DataFrame and an N_guides x N_barcodes confusion matrix are held, reads are streamed. STEP5 is thousands of independent CRISPResso2 invocations (one per guide per sample) and is the second-largest cost, minutes to an hour per sample, again one array task per sample. STEP6 is I/O-bound over the same thousands of directories, a minute or two per sample. A cluster is required for STEPs 4-6 — do not attempt them on a laptop. STEPs 7-9 are local and cheap: compiling, lane-merging and replicate-merging a 48-lane screen plus building the count matrix is seconds to a couple of minutes in a notebook, limited by reading a few hundred small CSVs. Expect the per-guide fastq and CRISPResso output trees to be the disk hog (one directory per guide per sample), so plan storage on the lab volume, not home.

designs.name: screen-stats
designs.description: Guide-level screen statistics for CRISPR base-editing / prime-editing sensor screens: RPM normalization with a +1 pseudocount, log2 fold-change against a T0-input or barcoding-screen baseline, replicate summaries (mean, median, concordant mean with a 2/3 directional-agreement threshold) and z-scores, a bootstrap empirical null built from the library's safe-targeting and non-targeting control guides (10,000 resamples per condition), two-sided empirical p-values per replicate, Fisher's and Stouffer's combination across replicates, and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR with FDR = min(FDR_high, FDR_low). Use this skill whenever asked to "calculate LFC and FDR", "run STEP9", "call hits", "which guides are enriched or depleted in bone marrow", "build the null distribution from control guides", "why does MAGeCK call so many hits", "add a new screen to the LFC pipeline", "re-run with spleen2 excluded", "make the LFC-FDR table for the ABE/CBE screen", or asked for empirical p-values, combined p-values, concordant mean LFC, or z-scores from a guide count matrix. It is the deliberately conservative, non-parametric alternative to MAGeCK for screens analyzed at the individual-guide level rather than collapsed to gene-level scores. It produces the per-screen `<screen>_LFC_FDR.csv` table that all downstream figure notebooks and the survival_comut / sci-plot work read.
designs.whenToUse: Fires once a guide × sample count matrix exists (STEP8 output) and the question is effect size or significance per guide — LFC, empirical p, combined p, FDR, hit calling, null-distribution QC, replicate exclusion sensitivity. It does not fire for upstream FASTQ handling, CRISPResso running, sensor-amplicon extraction or building the count matrix (that is ngs-screen), for designing the library or its control guides (library-design), for plotting the resulting table (sci-plot), or for mouse↔human variant mapping (h2m-variant).
coreCapabilities: Normalize a guide × sample count matrix to RPM with a +1 pseudocount per guide, via `rpm(df)`, which treats `df.columns[2:]` as the sample columns and requires `sgRNA` and `gene` as the first two columns.

Compute per-replicate log2 fold-change against either baseline mode, auto-detected: `baseline='t0'` (median RPM across `to_comparison_samps`, e.g. `['input']` or `['input_rep1','input_rep2','input_rep3']`) or `baseline='barcoding'` (per-condition median RPM across the matching barcoding-screen replicate columns in a second count table).

Summarize replicates per condition into `LFC_avg_*`, `LFC_median_*` and `LFC_concordant_mean_*` — the last being the mean over only those replicates agreeing with the majority sign, with guides below `ambiguity_threshold=2/3` directional agreement set to NaN and flagged in `LFC_directional_*`.
Convert each of the three LFC summaries to a z-score across all guides in that condition (`z_score_avg_*`, `z_score_median_*`, `z_score_concordant_mean_*`), computed on non-NaN values only.

Build a per-condition empirical null by pooling control-guide replicate LFCs (classifications `non-targeting control` + `safe-targeting control`) and bootstrap-resampling 10,000 values with replacement at a fixed seed, via `bootstrap_null`.
QC the null with `plot_null_distributions`, which overlays the bootstrapped histogram against each replicate's own control-guide LFC histogram per condition and optionally writes a PDF.
Compute two-sided empirical p-values per guide per replicate as p_high = (1 + #(null >= obs))/(1 + N) and p_low = (1 + #(null <= obs))/(1 + N), keeping the enrichment and depletion tails separate.

Combine replicate p-values per tail with both Fisher's and Stouffer's method via `scipy.stats.combine_pvalues`, BH-adjust each with `statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests(method='fdr_bh')`, and report `FDR_<cond>_fishers` / `FDR_<cond>_stouffers` as min(FDR_high, FDR_low).

Attach sensor editing measurements for every time point and condition from STEP7 MLE CSVs via `attach_editing_info`, pulling `Reads_aligned_all_amplicons`, `corr_perc`, `target_base_edit_perc`, `byproduct_INDEL_perc` and `byproduct_sub_perc` keyed on `Guide_ID` → `gRNA_id`, so LFC-vs-editing calibration is possible from the single output table.

Run the whole chain for one screen with `run_screen_pipeline` and for many screens from a `screens` dict, printing per-condition hit counts (Fisher, Stouffer, overlap at FDR<0.1, split into depleted/enriched at |LFC|>1) for a quick sanity read.

Aggregate per-sample CRISPResso `*_compact_unfiltered.csv` files into per-condition MLE CSVs honoring an explicit replicate-exclusion list, via `_mle_from_compact`, so that count-table exclusions and editing-table exclusions stay in sync.
Re-run a screen with replicates excluded and diff the hit calls, which is how the published sensitivity analyses (`ABE_FC_BC_T0_removed`, `ABE_FC_EPO_TO_BC_removed`) were produced.

gotchas: `rpm()` hardcodes `df.columns[2:]` as the sample columns, so the count matrix must have exactly two leading annotation columns named `sgRNA` and `gene`. An extra index column from a careless `to_csv`/`read_csv` round-trip silently turns an annotation column into a 'sample' and corrupts every RPM. Preflight this.

`two_sided_FDR` mutates `LFC_df` in place and returns the same object, so `run_screen_pipeline`'s `df_holder` ends up holding N aliases of one DataFrame (verified: `all(x is df)`). The pipeline only works because `pd.concat(df_holder, axis=1)` is followed by `.loc[:,~combined.columns.duplicated()].copy()`. Anyone refactoring this — reordering the loop, concatenating without the dedup, or caching an 'earlier' copy expecting it to lack later columns — will get wrong or duplicated output. The same dedup idiom in `LFC_table_generator` is the documented B-ALL pattern already in the user's memory.

Both `pd.merge(LFC, library, on='gRNA_id')` and the six sequential merges inside `attach_editing_info` are default INNER joins with no size assertion. A guide missing from the library annotation or from any single MLE CSV is dropped silently, and because the editing merges cascade, one bad condition file shrinks the whole table. On the ABE_OG fixture nothing drops (1070 in, 1070 out), which is exactly why the hazard goes unnoticed. Always print rows before and after.

The empirical p-value step is a pure-Python double loop calling `sum(null >= observed)` per guide per replicate: measured ~129 s per tail for 13,242 guides × 10 replicates, so ~4 min per condition and well over 20 min for a 5-condition CBE screen. `np.searchsorted` on the sorted null gives bit-identical results (verified on both tails, NaN included) in milliseconds. Ship the vectorized version but keep the loop available for an equivalence check.

FDR is computed over every row of the table, controls included, so `multipletests` is correcting across targeting and control guides together and control guides can themselves be called hits (2 of 36 controls reach FDR<0.1 in bone marrow in `ABE_OG_LFC_FDR.csv`). That is the published behavior — do not 'fix' it silently, but do state it, because a reader filtering hits without excluding controls will report control guides as biology.

Control-guide depth sets the resolution of the null: the p-value floor is 1/(n_bootstrap+1) ≈ 1e-4 regardless of how few real control observations there are. After the inner merge the ABE_OG fixture keeps only 36 control guides (26 safe-targeting + 10 non-targeting), so the 10,000-value bootstrap is resampling ~36 × n_reps underlying numbers. Bootstrapping cannot manufacture information it does not have — warn when the pooled control pool is small and always look at the `plot_null_distributions` QC panel.

`control_classes` matches `classification` on exact strings `'non-targeting control'` and `'safe-targeting control'`. A library whose labels differ in case, hyphenation or wording yields an empty `controls` frame; `bootstrap_null` then prints `0 control guide LFC values` and `np.random.choice` raises on an empty array. The focused library's `essential truncation guide` class is deliberately NOT a control — it is a positive control for depletion and must stay out of the null.

The concordant-mean sign vote breaks ties toward positive (`majority_positive = n_positive >= n_negative`), so a perfectly split 2-up/2-down guide is treated as 'positive' with frac_concordant 0.5, which then fails the 2/3 threshold and becomes NaN. Correct in effect, but anyone reading `LFC_directional_*` should know the tie rule rather than assume symmetry.

`LFC_concordant_mean_*` contains NaN for ambiguous guides by design. Downstream code that does `(hits[lfc_col] > 1)` silently treats NaN as False — fine for counting, but a `.mean()` or a volcano plot over that column drops ambiguous guides without saying so. The hit-count print block already guards with `if lfc_col not in hits.columns`, not for NaN.

Baseline mode is auto-detected solely by whether `df_counts_bc` is not None. Passing `to_comparison_samps` alongside `df_counts_bc` does not error — the T0 baseline is just ignored, and you get barcoding-mode numbers from a config that reads like T0. Config validation should reject that combination outright.

Replicate exclusions live in two places that must agree: the `samps_to_merge` lists (with reasons in comments, e.g. CBE_BC excludes bm1,2,6,8,10 and spleen1,2,6,8,10 for abnormal skewing) and the `groups` lists passed to `_mle_from_compact`. They are retyped by hand in the notebook and will drift, silently pairing LFCs from one replicate set with editing percentages from another. Drive both from one shared config.

`screens` entries can point at an MLE folder from a different arm: `ABE_FC_BC_T0` reads `MLE/focused/ABE_EPO` while `ABE_FC_BC_T0_removed` reads `MLE/focused/ABE_BC`. This may be intentional (EPO editing as the sensor reference) but it is undocumented in the notebook and is the single most confusing thing in the config. Have the skill echo which MLE folder each screen used.

Single-replicate conditions (`d5=['d5']`, `lib=['lib']`, `plasmidlib`) are valid — both Fisher and Stouffer pass a lone p-value through unchanged (verified) — but a one-replicate 'combined p-value' carries no replicate-consistency evidence and `np.std` based z-scores on one column are still computed across guides. Do not put `lib`/`plasmidlib` in `conditions_null`; the existing configs correctly do not.

`combine_pvalues` propagates NaN to NaN, and `multipletests` will then fail or produce NaN FDRs. NaN LFCs arise from zero baseline RPM — the +1 pseudocount in `rpm()` is what prevents it, so dropping or changing the pseudocount reintroduces -inf/NaN LFCs downstream.

Fisher and Stouffer both assume independent tests, which biological replicates sharing one initial guide pool violate. The docs flag this; the skill should repeat it rather than let FDR<0.1 be read as a calibrated error rate. Fisher is the reported default precisely because it is conventional, not because it is better behaved — it can call a hit on one extreme replicate, which is why the overlap count with Stouffer is printed.

The notebook's import cell pulls `upsetplot`, `adjustText`, `matplotlib_venn` and `sklearn.decomposition.PCA`, none of which the pipeline uses. Lifting that cell verbatim into the skill's scripts would make the FDR table unobtainable on a clean env for no reason. Import only numpy, pandas, scipy, statsmodels, matplotlib, seaborn, os.

`warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')` at the top of the notebook hides exactly the signals that matter here: pandas merge/dtype warnings, `RuntimeWarning: divide by zero` and `invalid value encountered` from `np.log2`, and `Mean of empty slice` from `np.nanmean`. Do not carry the blanket suppression into the scripts; suppress narrowly if at all.

`seed=0` and `n_bootstrap=10000` are what the published tables were produced with. Changing either moves p-values near the 1e-4 floor and will change hit counts, so pin them in config and record them in the output provenance.

The output CSV is one wide row per guide (152 columns for ABE_OG) with condition suffixes, not tidy long format. Downstream figure code selects by f-string column names, so renaming a condition (`bm` → `bonemarrow`) breaks every figure notebook. Treat `new_names` as a stable key.

Laptop-scale; no cluster needed. As written, the pure-Python empirical-p loop dominates: measured ~129 s per tail for a 13,242-guide × 10-replicate condition, i.e. ~4 min per condition and 20-25 min for a 5-condition OG screen, with the 10-screen `screens` dict running well over an hour. With the `np.searchsorted` vectorization the p-value step drops to milliseconds and a full screen finishes in seconds, making the ~10-screen sweep a sub-minute job; I/O of the MLE CSVs (14,412 rows × 6 conditions per screen) becomes the slowest part. Memory is modest: the largest count matrix here is 13,242 × 41, the null is 10,000 floats per condition, and the final table is ~13k × 152 — comfortably under ~1 GB. The vectorized p-value step materializes an n_guides × n_reps float array per tail (a few MB), so it does not change the profile. Plotting is the only interactive cost; writing the null PDF is instant.

designs.name: survival_comut
designs.description: Clinical cohort co-mutation and survival statistics on a patient x gene mutation table — Fisher's exact co-occurrence and mutual-exclusivity testing with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, Cox proportional-hazards hazard ratios for double-mutant vs single-mutant patient groups, log-rank tests, and Kaplan-Meier curves, plus the matching volcano / bubble / forest / masked-heatmap figures. Built for the MetaAML CH analysis (clonal hematopoiesis genes vs top recurrent AML drivers in `final_data_matrix.RData`) but takes any long-format cohort table with Sample, Gene, Time_to_OS and Censor columns, and works equally on AACR-GENIE or MSK-IMPACT pulls. Use whenever asked to "test co-occurrence", "are these genes mutually exclusive", "run Fisher on the cohort", "co-mutation analysis", "which co-mutations are significant", "fit a Cox model", "get the hazard ratio", "is this pair prognostic", "plot Kaplan-Meier", "KM curve for DNMT3A + RAD21", "make the co-occurrence volcano", "forest plot of significant pairs", "survival heatmap", "does CH co-mutation change outcome", or to redo any part of the CH committee-meeting clinical analysis. Not for designing variants or guides, not for pooled-screen LFC/FDR statistics, and not for querying raw public databases — those are h2m-variant, screen-stats and cohort_query.
designs.whenToUse: Fires when the unit of analysis is a *patient* and the question is co-occurrence/exclusivity or time-to-event outcome (Fisher OR, Cox HR, log-rank, KM); does not fire for guide- or variant-level statistics (screen-stats), for pulling cohorts out of GENIE/COSMIC in the first place (cohort_query), or for annotating variants (h2m-variant).
coreCapabilities: Load a cohort into the canonical long format: `pyreadr.read_r()` on an .RData matrix (the MetaAML `final_data_matrix`, 10302 rows x 28 cols) or a CSV/TSV, then coerce the 14 NUMERIC_COLUMNS (VAF, Age, Hemoglobin, Platelet, WBC, LDH, BM_blast_percent, PB_blast_percent, PB_wbc_percent, Time_to_OS, Censor, mut_freq_gene, mut_freq_pt, mut_freq_bin) with pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce').

Those 15 points land at log(OR) = -2.66 on every volcano, bubble and heatmap as if that were a measured effect size, when it actually means 'zero double-mutant patients'. Replace with `safe_log_or` from the sibling notebook and carry an explicit `or_floored` flag so these points can be shaped or annotated differently.

BH correction is applied WITHIN each focal gene (`groupby('ch_gene').transform(...)`), i.e. 20 tests per family, not 200 across the panel. designs.runtimeCharacter:
Seconds to about two minutes end to end on the MetaAML scale (2135 de novo patients, 10 focal x 20 comparator = 200 pairs); laptop-sized, single-core, well under 1 GB. No cluster.

Breakdown: `pyreadr.read_r` on the 10302 x 28 .RData is a few seconds. The 200 Fisher tests are the slow part only because `fisher_for_pair` rebuilds two full per-sample boolean Series and a `pd.crosstab` for every pair — O(pairs x samples) Python-level work, roughly 10-30 s. Switching to `build_binary_matrix` + `fisher_or_p_from_binary` from the sibling notebook makes this sub-second. The 200 `CoxPHFitter.fit` calls are each on a few hundred rows with one covariate, so about 20-60 s total. Figures dominate the wall clock: `adjust_text` is iterative and slow, and the 3x4 volcano grid calls it 10 times with `force_text=(2.0,2.0)` — budget 30-90 s for `co-occurrence.pdf` alone, more for the bubble plots whose `plot_ch_bubble` scatters points one at a time in a Python loop instead of a single vectorized `scatter`.

Scaling note: a GENIE-wide run (50+ genes against each other, thousands of samples) pushes the pair count into the thousands. There the per-pair crosstab becomes genuinely painful and the vectorized binary-matrix path is mandatory, but it is still minutes on a laptop, not cluster work. Memory stays modest because the patient x gene int8 matrix is tiny.

designs.name: library-design
designs.description: Design pegRNA and base-editing sgRNA libraries with PEGG (`pegg.prime.run`, `pegg.base.run_base`), including sensor cassettes, silent-bystander designs, OptiPrime efficiency scoring, synonymous-codon and safe-targeting/non-targeting controls, and the pooled oligo sequences to order. Use whenever asked to design a pegRNA library, design base-editing guides or sgRNAs for a variant list, "run PEGG", "run prime.run", "run run_base", pick ABE vs CBE guides for a mutation, add a sensor to guides, add silent bystanders, score pegRNAs with OptiPrime or PEGG2_Score, add safe-targeting / non-targeting / silent controls to a pool, work out how many guides per mutation a library will have, or audit that designed bystanders really are synonymous. Also fires for "design guides for these mutations", "make me a CH/AML pegRNA library", "which PBS and RTT lengths should I enumerate", "why did my variant drop out of the library", and "turn MUTATION_DESIGN.csv into a library". This skill ends at the pooled oligo table; hand its output to `pegrna-oligo` for individually ordered Golden Gate oligos.
designs.whenToUse: Fires when guides/pegRNAs must be *designed* from a variant table — choosing PAM sites, RTT/PBS lengths, sensors, bystanders, controls, and efficiency scores. Does not fire for human→mouse variant modeling (h2m-variant), for cohort variant frequency (cohort_query), for converting an already-finished design table into individually ordered Golden Gate oligos (pegrna-oligo), or for analyzing screen readout (ngs-screen, screen-stats).
coreCapabilities: Design pegRNAs for any variant class (SNP, ONP/DNP/TNP, INS, DEL, INDEL) with `pegg.prime.run(input_df, input_format, chrom_dict=...)`, enumerating every PAM site x RTT length x PBS length and returning PAM, PAM_strand, Protospacer (G+19), RTT, PBS, RTT_PBS, Distance_to_nick, RHA_size, PAM_disrupted, Proto_disrupted.

Design base-editing sgRNAs with `pegg.base.run_base(...)`, which auto-filters the input to SNPs, splits them into ABE (A>G on + / T>C on -) and CBE (C>T on + / G>A on -) with an `Editor` column, and labels protospacer position 1-20 (`Protospacer_Location`) plus `Ideal_Edit_Window` against `ideal_edit_window=[4,8]`.
Design arbitrary non-ABE/CBE editors by passing `filtration=['C>G','T>A',...]` to `run_base`, which sets `Editor` to the requested substitution string.
Attach a sensor cassette to every design (`sensor=True`), with `sensor_wt`, `sensor_alt`, `sensor_orientation`, and a `sensor_error` column naming designs whose sensor could not be built.

Design pegRNAs carrying extra synonymous ('silent bystander') mutations alongside the intended edit via `silent_bystander=True`, returning both plain and bystander designs in one table separated by `has_silent_bystander`, with `n_bystander_muts`, `bystander_positions`, `bystander_dist_to_edit`, `PAM_disrupted_edit`, `PAM_disrupted_by_bystander`.

Resolve per-row reading frame for a multi-gene library with `bystander.cds_for_variants(df, db)` (canonical transcript per Hugo_Symbol) or `bystander.add_cds_to_variants(df, db, tx_column='tx_id_m')` (use the transcript H2M already chose), then validate it with `bystander.cds_annotation_report()` before designing.

Score pegRNAs on an absolute efficiency scale with `optiprime=True` / `rankby='OptiPrime_Score'` (predicted fraction of alleles carrying the intended edit), or on PEGG's own `PEGG2_Score` (weighted linear regression) / `RF_Score` (random forest), both built on `OnTarget_Azimuth_Score` from Rule Set 2.

Build control arms: `library.safe_muts(n, chrom_dict, organism=)` (Morgens 2017 safe regions), `library.nontargeting_guides(n, edit_type='prime'|'base')` (max 1000, human only), `library.aavs1_muts(chrom_dict, n, genome_version=)`, `library.neutral_substitutions(gene, chrom, strand, start_end_cds, chrom_dict)` (all synonymous substitutions in a gene), and `library.library_maker()` to assemble variants + silent + safe at chosen fractions.

Build a same-codon synonymous-control library (swap each variant's codon for the synonymous codon differing at fewest bases) and design it through a second `prime.run()` call with identical parameters, so controls span the same efficiency range as the real designs.
Filter the design pool: drop `contains_polyT_terminator == True`, drop `contains_RE_site` / designs containing BsmBI `CGTCTC`, and drop `sensor_error == 'sensor too small; ...'`.

Emit pooled oligos with `prime.prime_oligo_generator(peg_df, epeg=True, epeg_motif='tevopreQ1'|'mpknot'|<seq>)` -> `pegRNA_oligo`, or `base.base_oligo_generator(peg_df)` -> `gRNA_oligo`; both assemble 5' adapter + protospacer + scaffold + (extension + epeg) + TTTTTTT + sensor + 3' adapter, with every part overridable.

Audit that designed bystanders really are synonymous: splice each `RTT` back onto the CDS, re-translate, and compare each bystander design's protein against the protein the plain designs for that same mutation agree on (works for missense, nonsense and frameshift alike).
Visualize one design's sensor with annotated bystander positions via `prime.sensor_viz(df_w_sensor, i)` / `base.sensor_viz_base(...)`.
Report library composition and the cost of an efficiency cutoff: genes, mutations, pegRNAs per mutation by design type, OptiPrime score distribution, and the mutation-coverage-vs-cutoff curve.
designs.inputs:
**A variant table in one of three `input_format`s.**

`'cBioPortal'` (the one to use for a real library; the only one that gives genomic coordinates, splice-site checks and a per-row reading frame) requires MAF column names: `Hugo_Symbol`, `Chromosome`, `Start_Position`, `End_Position`, `Variant_Type` (`SNP`/`DNP`/`TNP`/`ONP`/`INS`/`DEL`/`INDEL`), `Reference_Allele`, `Tumor_Seq_Allele2`. `Chromosome` must be `int` for 1-22 and the strings `'X'`/`'Y'` — no `chr` prefix — because `chrom_dict` is keyed that way. H2M output needs renaming first (`gene_name_m`→`Hugo_Symbol`, `chr_m`→`Chromosome`, `start_m`→`Start_Position`, `end_m`→`End_Position`, `ref_seq_m`→`Reference_Allele`, `alt_seq_m`→`Tumor_Seq_Allele2`, `type_m`→`Variant_Type`).

`'WT_ALT'` needs columns `WT` and `ALT`; `'PrimeDesign'` needs column `SEQ` in PrimeDesign bracket notation. Neither carries coordinates, so both need `ORF_start` (0/1/2) for bystanders and cannot have splice sites checked.

**A reference genome as `chrom_dict`** — required for `'cBioPortal'` input; `prime.run` asserts on it. Either `prime.genome_loader('$LAB_DATA_ROOT/RefGenome/.../*.fna.gz')` (returns `(chrom_dict, filtered_descriptions)`) or, when H2M already loaded the genome, build it from `h2m.genome_loader` records by regexing `chromosome (\w+)` out of each record description. The build must match the variant coordinates: GRCh37 for v19 annotation, GRCm39 for vm33.

**A GENCODE annotation `.db`** — only for silent bystanders — loaded as a `gffutils.FeatureDB` (`h2m.anno_loader($LAB_DATA_ROOT/Genecode/gencode_vm33_GRCm39.db)`). Same build as the genome.

**Optionally an OptiPrime install**, reached through `OPTIPRIME_SRC` and `OPTIPRIME_PYTHON`, or the `optiprime_src=` / `optiprime_python=` arguments.
designs.outputs:

designs.runtimeCharacter:
**Design itself is minutes.** Genome load ~20 s and a few GB of RAM (`chrom_dict` holds whole chromosome sequences); GENCODE `.db` load is seconds. The per-mutation PAM/RTT/PBS enumeration is pure Python and runs at roughly a second or two per variant for a 40-variant library — a few minutes for the whole table.

**Scoring is the expensive step, and it is the only one.** OptiPrime costs ~0.2155 s per pegRNA per worker (most of it featurization), plus ~20 s of JAX JIT startup per worker, and `score()` will not shard below 500 rows. The CH/AML main library (665k pegRNAs, bystanders on, `pegRNAs_per_mut='All'`, `optiprime_prefilter=None`) took **~6.5 h on 7 workers**; the silent-control library another **~4.4 h**. Near-linear in cores, so `optiprime_jobs = cores - 1`. With `optiprime=False` and only `PEGG2_Score`/`RF_Score`, the whole run is minutes — Azimuth is called once per unique `Protospacer_30`, not per pegRNA.

**Memory and disk, not CPU, are the usual wall.** 665k rows x ~70 columns is ~1.45 GB in memory as a pandas frame, and the two libraries together are 2.9 GB of plain CSV. Write gzipped (~2-8% of raw) and checkpoint immediately.

**The bystander audit is the other long pole** and needs the per-transcript cache: the naive per-pegRNA version (`list(str(chrom_seq))` on a ~182 Mb chromosome) ran for hours, and auditing all 665k rows would take ~3 h even cached. Audit a bounded random sample per mutation instead — the failure mode is systematic per mutation, not a 1-2% sprinkle.

**No cluster required.** Everything above ran on an 8-core macOS laptop. A cluster helps only by giving OptiPrime more cores; nothing here needs a scheduler, and a long scoring run should be launched with checkpoints rather than split across nodes.

designs.name: h2m-variant
designs.description: Models human genetic variants in the mouse genome (and the reverse) using the bioh2m package — takes a variant in MAF/VCF/ClinVar/cBioPortal form, finds the mouse ortholog and canonical transcript, and computes the exact murine nucleotide change that reproduces the human protein effect, including alternative codon-level strategies when the identical nucleotide change does not work, base-editing-compatible modeling, and a per-variant alignment plot. Use whenever asked to "model this human variant in mouse", "what is the mouse equivalent of TP53 R273H", "mouse-ify these mutations", "run H2M", "h2m this MAF", "can this variant be modeled in mice", "is this base-editable in mouse", "what's the mouse codon for this amino acid change", "find the mouse ortholog and transcript for these genes", "convert these GENIE/ClinVar/gnomAD variants to mouse coordinates", "which of these variants are class 0 vs class 3", or "make the H2M alignment figure for this variant". Also fires for the reverse direction (mouse variant to human equivalent, direction='m2h') and for paralog modeling within one species (direction='h2h' or 'm2m', e.g. SMARCA2 to SMARCA4). This skill ends at the modeled variant coordinates — it does not design pegRNAs or sgRNAs (that is library-design), does not query cohort frequencies (cohort_query), and does not analyze sequencing data.
designs.whenToUse: Fires when the task is converting a variant between human and mouse (or between paralogs) at nucleotide/codon resolution, or judging whether a variant is modelable at all. Does not fire for pegRNA/sgRNA design, cohort frequency queries, NGS analysis, or survival/comut plots — those are library-design, cohort_query, ngs-screen, survival_comut.
coreCapabilities: Loads the four heavy reference objects once per session — `h2m.genome_loader(path)` returns `(records, index_list)` for human and mouse FASTA .fna.gz, and `h2m.anno_loader(path)` returns a `gffutils.FeatureDB` from a prebuilt GENCODE .db — and keeps them in memory for all downstream calls (~3 min, several GB).

Queries human/mouse gene orthologs with `h2m.query(id, direction='h2m'|'m2h', ty='name'|'gene_id'|'tx_id')`, returning a list of dicts with mouse gene name, gene id, homology type (one2one / one2many / many2many) and percent sequence similarity; `h2m.query_batch(df, direction)` does the same for a DataFrame keyed on `gene_name_h` (or `gene_name_m` for m2h) and returns `[df_ok, df_failed]`, fanning out one row per ortholog when a gene has several.

Resolves canonical transcripts: `h2m.get_tx_id(id, species, ver=37|38)` hits the live Ensembl REST API (grch37.rest.ensembl.org or rest.ensembl.org) and returns `[chr, start, end, canonical_tx, list_of_all_tx, tx_dic_list]` with the canonical transcript moved to index 0; `h2m.get_tx_batch(df, species, ver)` is offline — it reads the packaged `dict_tx_h.json`/`dict_tx_m.json` and writes `tx_id_h`+`ref_genome_h` or `tx_id_m`, returning `[df_ok, df_failed]`.

Models a single variant with `h2m.model(records_h, index_list_h, records_m, index_list_m, db_h, db_m, tx_id_h, tx_id_m, start, end, ref_seq, alt_seq, ty_h=..., ver=37)`, returning a LIST of dicts (one per alternative, up to `max_alternative=5`) with the 44-key schema including `status`, `class`, `statement`, `classification_h`, `exon_h`, `HGVSc_h`/`HGVSp_h`, the original-modeling mouse variant (`start_m_ori`,`end_m_ori`,`ref_seq_m_ori`,`alt_seq_m_ori`,`HGVSc_m_ori`,`HGVSp_m_ori`) and the amino-acid-matched alternative (`start_m`,`end_m`,`ref_seq_m`,`alt_seq_m`,`HGVSc_m`,`HGVSp_m`).

Interprets and filters the H2M result classes, which are the whole point of the output: class 0 = originally modelable with the identical nucleotide change; class 1 = alternatively modelable (different codon, same amino acid); class 2 = modelable but effect may not be consistent (frameshift and non-coding — no amino-acid-matched alternative exists); class 3 = not originally modelable and no alternative found; class 4 = input ref_seq disagrees with the genome (`match == False`); class 5 = coordinate error, variant not in the query gene; class 6 = not originally modelable (internal gate, surfaces with `param='BE'`).

Runs base-editing-only modeling with `param='BE'`, which gates every candidate through `BE_check`/`GateBE` so only same-length, single-base-species transitions in `be_tuple = [('A','G'),('T','C'),('C','T'),('G','A')]` survive (AA to GG passes, AC to GT does not) — and returns alternative BE strategies even for variants that were already class 0.

Accepts amino-acid-level input with `coor='aa'`: pass the residue number as both `start` and `end` and the one-letter codes as `ref_seq`/`alt_seq` (e.g. `175, 175, 'R', 'H', coor='aa', ty_h='SNP'`), and H2M reconstructs the nucleotide reference itself and sets `match=False` if the translated reference disagrees.

Batch-models a whole table with `h2m.model_batch(df, records_h, index_list_h, records_m, index_list_m, db_h, db_m, ver, ...)`, which sorts by `(tx_id_h, tx_id_m)`, computes the protein alignment once per transcript pair via `get_tx_and_align`, and returns `[df_result, df_failed]`; `bind=True` merges the non-coordinate columns of the input back onto the result by `index`.

Normalizes public variant data into H2M's MAF input: `h2m.cbio_reader(path)` for cBioPortal/TCGA/AACR-GENIE `data_mutations*.txt` (renames Hugo_Symbol to gene_name_h, HGVSc to tx_id_h, Start_Position to start_h, End_Position to end_h, Variant_Type to type_h, Reference_Allele to ref_seq_h, Tumor_Seq_Allele2 to alt_seq_h); `h2m.vcf_reader(path)` + `h2m.vcf_to_maf(df)` for gnomAD browser CSV exports; `h2m.clinvar_reader(path, list_of_ids)` + `h2m.clinvar_to_maf(df)` for the ClinVar vcf.gz; and `h2m.get_variant_type(df, ref_col, alt_col, col_name='type_h')` to infer SNP/DNP/TNP/ONP/INS/DEL from allele lengths.

Draws the per-variant alignment figure with `h2m.visualization(model_result, flank_size=N, print_size=M)`, which requires the model call to have been made with `show_sequence=True` (that adds `seq_h`, `new_seq_h`, `seq_m`, `new_seq_m_ori`, `new_seq_m`, `human_tx_idx`, `human_p_idx`, `mouse_tx_idx`, `mouse_p_idx`, `dist_h`, `dist_m`).

Reports local homology confidence via `flank_size_left` / `flank_size_right` — the number of identical bases shared between human and mouse immediately flanking the variant — which is the field to cite when judging how much to trust a given modeling.

Reverses direction (`direction='m2h'`) by passing mouse coordinates in the `start`/`end`/`ref_seq`/`alt_seq` slots; `replace_keys` then swaps every `_h`/`_m` suffix in the output dict. Models paralogs within one species by passing the same genome and db twice with `direction='h2h'` or `'m2m'`, which suffixes output columns `_1`/`_2` instead.

gotchas: `h2m.model` returns a LIST of dicts, not a dict — one entry per alternative modeling, up to `max_alternative` (default 5). `pd.DataFrame(model_result)` gives you N rows for ONE input variant. Anyone treating the return as a single record silently analyzes only the first alternative, and anyone counting rows of a `model_batch` result overcounts variants. Deduplicate or group on `index` before counting.

Two different mouse variants are reported per row and they are not interchangeable. `*_m_ori` is the result of making the IDENTICAL nucleotide change in the mouse genome; `*_m` (no suffix) is the alternative that reproduces the same AMINO ACID change, possibly via a different codon. For class 0 they are the same; for class 1 they differ and `*_m` is the one you order. For class 2 and 3 the amino-acid match does not exist. Picking `start_m`/`alt_seq_m` blindly for a class 2 frameshift or non-coding variant gives you something whose protein effect H2M explicitly does not vouch for.

`class` 4 and 5 are input errors, not biology. Class 5 means the coordinate is not inside the query transcript — almost always a GRCh37/GRCh38 mismatch between the coordinates, the `ver` argument and the annotation .db. Class 4 (`match == False`) means the reference allele you supplied disagrees with the genome at that position, usually a strand mistake: coordinates and alleles must be given on the POSITIVE strand of the chromosome even when the transcript is on the minus strand — `model` reverse-complements internally. Always check the class distribution before interpreting any result.

`model_batch` swallows every per-variant exception. Both the alignment step and the per-variant `model` call sit inside bare `try/except`, and failures are just appended to `error_list` and returned as the second DataFrame. The function prints only 'There were rows that could not be processed.' You get no traceback and no reason. Always inspect `df_failed` and, to debug, re-run those rows one at a time through `h2m.model` where the exception surfaces.

`memory_protect=True` (the default) raises 'Alarm 3' whenever either protein is longer than `memory_size=10000` aa, because the pairwise alignment can kill the kernel. Long genes (TTN, DMD, OBSCN) hit this. The lab's own production run uses `memory_size=2000` (methods/run_h2m/h2m_db.py) to fail fast on big genes rather than risk the node. Lowering the number makes it stricter, not looser; `memory_protect=False` is what lifts the cap, and only do that with real memory to spare.

`genome_loader` reads the whole FASTA into memory as a list of Biopython records — the source comment says ~4 GB for human, ~3 minutes, and you need human AND mouse simultaneously. Load once per session and reuse `(records_h, index_list_h, records_m, index_list_m, db_h, db_m)`. Never put the load inside a loop or a per-variant helper.

Chromosome handling is positional and silently wrong for the wrong species. `GetChrSeq` indexes `records[index_list[chrom-1]]` and maps X/Y to hardcoded integers that differ between species: human X=22, Y=23; mouse X=19, Y=20. `get_tx_id` applies the same remap to its returned `chr`. Passing a mouse genome where a human one is expected does not error — it returns sequence from the wrong chromosome. This is also why the reference FASTA must be the exact NCBI file (alternate/unplaced/unlocalized/patch contigs are filtered by description keyword) and not a differently sorted assembly.

`get_tx_id` requires internet and hits Ensembl REST; `get_tx_batch` does not. `get_tx_batch` reads the packaged `dict_tx_h.json`/`dict_tx_m.json` shipped inside the installed wheel, so it is fast and offline but FROZEN at bioh2m 1.0.3 — a gene renamed since then lands in `df_failed`, not in the result. For human it picks `dict_tx_h[gene][0]` for ver=37 and `[1]` for ver=38; the index is silently positional, so a wrong `ver` yields a transcript ID from the wrong assembly. Mouse is GRCm39 only; `get_tx_id` for mouse ignores `ver` and always uses rest.ensembl.org.

`param='BE'` is stricter than 'it is a transition'. `BE_check` requires `all_characters_same(ref)` AND `all_characters_same(alt)` AND equal lengths AND `(ref[0], alt[0]) in be_tuple` — so A to G, AA to GG and CCC to TTT pass, but AC to GT and any indel do not. Variants failing the gate come back as class 6 with status False, which is a DIFFERENT class value from the class 3 you get in default mode; filter on class accordingly.

`query` RAISES rather than returning empty for an unknown gene: an unrecognized gene name, or a gene id absent from the packaged `human_name_dict.json`, throws ValueError. Only a gene that is in the name dict but has no entry in `homo_dict` returns `[None]`. Wrap single-gene queries in try/except, or use `query_batch`, which partitions cleanly into `[df_ok, df_failed]`. `query(direction='m2h')` additionally accepts ONLY gene names — a mouse gene id or transcript id raises 'Error 2' — and `query_batch` in m2h mode reads the column `gene_name_m`, not `gene_name_h`.

A one-to-many ortholog relationship multiplies your rows. `query_batch` emits one row per human-to-mouse pair and merges with `how='outer'`, so a human gene with two mouse orthologs becomes two rows, each of which then becomes up to `max_alternative` rows after modeling. Track your original variant identity through the `index` column from the start.

`model_batch` requires a column literally named `index` and uses it as the join key for `bind=True` and the alternative grouping. A DataFrame whose identifier sits in the pandas index rather than a column fails 'Error 2'; `df.reset_index()` first. The ClinVar path in the tutorial renames `ID` to `index` for exactly this reason. Duplicate `index` values corrupt the `bind=True` merge into a cartesian product.

Column-name conventions shift with `direction` and will break any hardcoded column list. `replace_keys` rewrites every `human`/`mouse` prefix and `_h`/`_m` suffix for `direction='m2h'`, and `h2h`/`m2m` paralog mode produces `_h_1`/`_h_2` suffixed columns (`gene_name_h_1`, `HGVSp_h_2`) instead. Read the actual `df.columns` after the call rather than assuming the h2m names.

`visualization` silently needs `show_sequence=True` on the model call. Without it the extra `seq_h`/`new_seq_m`/`*_idx` keys are absent and the plot call fails or draws nothing useful. The two calls must be made as a pair for the same variant.

INS coordinates are rewritten in place. `check_mut_info` shifts `start_h -= 1` and `end_h += 1` for an INS with a non-empty ref, and `final_return` shifts them back — so the INS convention in and out is the MAF one (`start`/`end` flanking the insertion point, `ref_seq='-'`), not VCF. Do not hand VCF-style INS/DEL rows to `model` directly; run them through `vcf_to_maf` or `clinvar_to_maf` first, which do the base-trimming and the start/end arithmetic correctly and set `format='MAF'` as a marker.

`get_variant_type` mutates its input DataFrame in place (it assigns `df_change = df` and then writes columns) and fills NaN alleles with `''`, which makes a length-0 ref read as DEL/INS rather than erroring. Pass a `.copy()` if you need the original. It also classifies any `len(ref) != len(alt)` as a plain INS/DEL with no frame check — the In_Frame vs Frame_Shifting call is made later inside `model` by `if_in_frame`.

`module.py` calls `warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")` at import time, globally, for the whole Python process. Importing bioh2m silences pandas and numpy warnings in every other library in the same session. Worth knowing when h2m is imported in a notebook alongside analysis code you expect to warn.

`model` uses module-level `global status, error, statement` to carry the class decision between its gate functions. It is not thread-safe and must not be parallelized inside one process. Scale out with the SLURM array pattern in methods/run_h2m/task.sh (split the input CSV, one process per shard) rather than with threads or a process pool sharing the loaded genome.

The tutorial, README and methods notebooks are full of hardcoded `/Users/kexindong/Documents/GitHub/Database/...` and `/Users/kexindong/Documents/GitHub/Output/...` paths, and `methods/run_h2m/h2m_db.py` hardcodes bare filenames that only resolve inside one cluster directory. None of these exist for the PI or other lab members. Every path in the skill must come from `$LAB_DATA_ROOT`, and the skill should fail with a single clear line naming the missing file rather than letting `genome_loader` die three minutes in on a gzip error.

The .db files are not downloadable artifacts of bioh2m — they are gffutils databases someone built once with `gffutils.create_db` from a GENCODE .gtf.gz. The versions the pipeline expects are `gencode_v19_GRCh37.db` and `gencode_vm33_GRCm39.db`. A .db built from a different GENCODE release has different transcript IDs and versions than `dict_tx_h.json` returns, which surfaces as a KeyError inside `GetTx` (`db_input[tx_id]`) rather than as a helpful message. Keep the .db release and the transcript-ID source in sync.
`methods/run_h2m/h2m_db.py` still does `import h2m`, the pre-rename module name. The package is now `bioh2m` and is imported as `import bioh2m as h2m` — lift the logic, not that import line.
designs.runtimeCharacter: Session setup dominates: `genome_loader` for both species takes ~3 minutes and several GB of RAM (~4 GB for the human records alone), and both genomes plus both gffutils DBs must be resident at once — budget 8-16 GB and load exactly once per session. After that, a single `h2m.model` call is sub-second to a few seconds. `model_batch` cost is driven by the number of distinct (tx_id_h, tx_id_m) pairs, not the number of variants, because the protein pairwise alignment is computed once per pair and reused via `align_input`; a few hundred variants across a handful of genes is seconds to a minute, while thousands of variants across thousands of genes is hours and is what the lab runs on the cluster as a 16-way SLURM array (methods/run_h2m/task.sh) with `memory_size=2000` to fail fast on very long proteins. `get_tx_id` is one network round-trip per gene and is the bottleneck if looped over many genes — use the offline `get_tx_batch` instead. Laptop is fine for interactive single-variant and gene-panel work; cluster is needed only for cohort-scale (GENIE/COSMIC-wide) runs.

designs.name: cohort_query
designs.description: Query clinical cancer cohorts — AACR-GENIE (v13.1–v18.0), MSK-IMPACT (msk_impact_2017), MSK-HEME (heme_msk_impact_2022) and COSMIC (Cancer Gene Census + MutantCensus v99 GRCh37) — for how often a variant or gene is mutated in patients, which cancer types carry it, and which genes co-mutate or are mutually exclusive. Loads the MAF-style cBioPortal tables, restricts to a disease cohort by CANCER_TYPE or CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED, collapses recurrent variants into one row per variant with a per-patient sample count, falls back from a disease-specific cohort to pan-cancer GENIE when a requested variant is absent, runs Fisher's exact co-mutation tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR on a patient x gene binary matrix, annotates genes with their COSMIC Role in Cancer, and draws per-gene mutation-position profiles in two cohorts side by side. Use this skill whenever asked "how common is DNMT3A R882H", "how many AML patients have FLT3-ITD", "what's the frequency of this variant in GENIE", "pull the top recurrent mutations in TET2", "which genes co-occur with TP53 in B-ALL", "is SRSF2 mutually exclusive with SF3B1", "co-mutation volcano", "odds ratio heatmap", "get me a MAF table of B-ALL variants to design a library against", "look this variant up in COSMIC", or any request to count, rank, or cross-tabulate patient variants from a clinical genomics cohort. It is the front end that produces the variant table other skills consume. It does NOT convert variants to mouse (h2m-variant), design guides or pegRNAs (library-design, pegrna-oligo), or fit survival models (survival_comut).
designs.whenToUse: Fires when the question is "how often / in whom / with what does this variant or gene occur in patients" and the answer comes from GENIE, MSK-IMPACT, MSK-HEME or COSMIC; does NOT fire for human-to-mouse variant conversion, guide/pegRNA design, screen readout statistics, or Cox/Kaplan-Meier survival work (those are h2m-variant, library-design, ngs-screen/screen_stats, survival_comut).
coreCapabilities: Resolve and load any of the four cohorts from $LAB_DATA_ROOT using the exact read_csv contract the working notebooks use (sep='\t', comment='#', na_values='Not Applicable'), which is what transparently skips cBioPortal's four '#' metadata lines and MSK-HEME's '#genome_nexus_version' / '#isoform' lines.

The cell-11 fisher_or_p_from_binary() does not do this. Use the cell-11 version and keep calc_odds_ratio only as a documented trap. Worse, the notebook then drops those NaNs and FDR-corrects the survivors, so q-values from that path are computed on a biased subset of tests.

fisher_for_pair() in CH.ipynb cell 6 substitutes the literal magic number 0.06982398 when the odds ratio is exactly 0, and 1.0 when it is NaN, purely so log(OR) plots without an infinity. That is a plotting hack, not a statistic — never let it reach a reported effect size. Prefer safe_log_or(eps=1e-12, cap=50) from the co-mutation notebook, which at least caps symmetrically and announces that it is capping.

A frequency without its denominator is a bug. The same variant is '3 patients' in MSK-HEME AML (296 samples) and '68 patients' in pan-cancer GENIE (~200k samples) — FLT3 p.D593_F594insNS literally is 0 and 68. Every number must carry cohort, version, disease filter and sample N. Selection belongs on the disease-relevant cohort; the pan-cancer cohort is a recurrence check, not a frequency source, and ch_aml_mutation_list.ipynb cell 11 says so in a comment for exactly this reason.

per_sample=True in filter_variants is not cosmetic: without it a patient sequenced twice (two Tumor_Sample_Barcodes, or primary plus relapse) counts twice and inflates the variant's frequency. GENIE sample IDs are GENIE-[CENTER]-[PATIENT]-[SAMPLE], so patient-level counting needs '-'.join(sample_id.split('-')[:3]) — which is what the 02/03 scripts do and what filter_variants' sample-level nunique does NOT do. Decide, and state on the output, whether a count is per-sample or per-patient.

GENIE v17 is GRCh37 only (NCBI_Build is uniformly GRCh37) and the local COSMIC is Cosmic_MutantCensus_v99_GRCh37. So every downstream H2M call must pass ver=37 — h2m.get_tx_batch(df, species='h', ver=37) and h2m.model_batch(..., 37) — paired with the GRCh37 genome GCF_000001405.25_GRCh37.p13 and gencode_v19_GRCh37.db. Handing GRCh37 coordinates to a GRCh38 annotation produces plausible-looking wrong variants, not an error.

The two COSMIC products are unrelated tables with unrelated schemas. The Cancer Gene Census csv has human-readable headers ('Gene Symbol', 'Role in Cancer') and is what get_cosmic_role() reads; Cosmic_MutantCensus_v99_GRCh37.tsv has UPPER_SNAKE headers (GENE_SYMBOL, MUTATION_AA, GENOMIC_WT_ALLELE, GENOME_START) and is 500 MB uncompressed. Neither uses MAF column names. Also, get_cosmic_role() takes .values[0] on the first matching row, so a gene with several census rows gets whichever sorted first, and t_dict.get(..., 'Undefined') silently maps any role string a future COSMIC release adds to 'Undefined' — the seven keys currently covered are the complete v2024 set, so a new release needs the dict updated rather than the default relied on.

HGVSp_Short matching is exact string matching and the strings are not canonical. DNMT3A R882H is 'p.R882H' in GENIE but a user will type 'R882H'; cell 17 handles this by passing protein_change=['p.R882H','R882H']. Frameshifts carry their new stop ('p.G646Wfs*12', 'p.Q652Rfs*48'), so 'p.G646Wfs' matches nothing. aa_position() simply regexes the first integer out of the string, which is right for 'p.R882H' and gives 577 for 'p.Q577_M578insSPE' — meaning an insertion is plotted at its left anchor residue only.

It belongs under $LAB_DATA_ROOT/PublicDatabase/COSMIC/ with a stable name; the skill should look there and only there, and must not be taught the old path.

Design constraints leak backwards into variant selection and must be stated rather than rediscovered. ch_aml_mutation_list.ipynb cell 74 shows the four most frequent FLT3 ITDs in MSK-HEME AML (78, 24, 36, 51 nt) all yield zero pegRNAs, because RTT<=30 minus min_RHA_size=8 leaves ~21 nt for the insert (ITD_MAX_INS_NT = 21) — and p.D593_Y597dup fails at only 15 nt anyway, because the nearest PAM forces a left homology arm >=13 nt. 'Most frequent' and 'designable' are therefore different queries: cohort_query should return the frequency ranking honestly and flag insertion length, leaving the designability verdict to library_design.

GENIE v17's data_mutations_extended.txt is ~3 GB and both source notebooks load it whole with pd.read_csv before filtering — multi-GB of RAM and tens of seconds to minutes on a laptop. Prefer usecols= plus a Hugo_Symbol or Tumor_Sample_Barcode pre-filter, or chunked reading, and cache the disease-restricted subset as .csv.gz (as early-leukemia-evolution already does for its other large tables) rather than re-reading the full MAF each session.

The skill reads from $LAB_DATA_ROOT and writes derived tables only; the repo's .gitignore should cover cohort .txt dumps, and the skill should say so in its instructions.
designs.runtimeCharacter: A targeted lookup (one gene, one cohort) is seconds once the MAF is in memory; the dominant cost is loading GENIE v17 data_mutations_extended.txt at ~3 GB — tens of seconds to a few minutes and several GB of RAM with the notebooks' plain pd.read_csv, so cache the disease-restricted subset. MSK-HEME and MSK-IMPACT load in seconds. COSMIC MutantCensus v99 is 500 MB uncompressed, roughly 10-30 s. Co-mutation is quadratic in genes and linear in patients but trivial at realistic sizes: 8 CH genes vs 50 comparison genes over ~1400 GENIE leukemia samples is a few seconds, and a full 50x50 pairwise matrix stays well under a minute. Per-gene profile PDFs are ~1 s each. Everything runs on a laptop; no cluster needed, and the only real constraint is RAM for the GENIE MAF.

designs.name: genotyping
designs.description: Turn bench genotyping readouts into quantitative calls and publication panels — Sanger .ab1 chromatogram traces into nucleotide and amino-acid sequence logos that read out editing efficiency and bystander edits at a codon, and FlowJo gate-statistic .xls exports into per-population frequencies, absolute cell counts and stacked/grouped bar plots. Reads base proportions directly from the ABI trace channels (DATA9-12 at PLOC1 peak positions), handles reverse-complement primers, labels the x-axis by amino-acid residue number, and collapses the 64 codon probabilities into per-residue amino-acid proportions so a heterozygous or partially edited codon is quantified rather than eyeballed. Use whenever asked to "call the edit from Sanger", "did the PE/BE edit work", "quantify editing from the ab1", "make a sequence logo from the chromatogram", "check for bystander editing", "what fraction is R248Q", "read out the genotyping", "plot the flow data", "parse the FlowJo export", "what percent LSK", "LSK fold expansion", or to turn an .ab1 folder or a flow statistics .xls into figures. For amplicon NGS editing quantification use ngs-screen/CRISPResso2 instead — this skill is for single-amplicon Sanger and gate-table flow, not FASTQ.
designs.whenToUse: Fires for single-amplicon Sanger .ab1 edit calling (editing %, bystander edits, codon-level AA logos) and for FlowJo gate-statistic .xls exports (population frequencies, absolute counts, expansion plots); it does not fire for FASTQ-based amplicon quantification (ngs-screen/CRISPResso2), for designing the edit (library-design/pegrna_oligo), or for raw .fcs files, which it cannot read.
coreCapabilities: Read an ABI .ab1 file and compute per-position A/C/G/T proportions from the raw trace channels (FWO_1 channel order, DATA9-DATA12 sampled at PLOC1 peak indices), not from the single called base, so a mixed/edited position is quantified.
Plot a nucleotide sequence logo over a user-specified 1-based start..end window of the AB1-called sequence (PBAS1), with logomaker color_scheme='classic'.
Reverse-complement a window for reverse-primer reads (row reversal plus base-column complement) so forward and reverse reads of the same locus give the same logo.

Collapse each codon's three base distributions across all 64 codons, translate with Bio.Seq.Seq.translate(), and plot an amino-acid logo (color_scheme='chemistry'), returning the per-residue AA proportion DataFrame for numeric readout of edit fraction and bystander amino acids.

Label the logo x-axis with real amino-acid residue numbers via aa_anno_range=(first_aa, last_aa) — ticks at codon centers (3*i+1) for nt logos, one tick per codon for aa logos — with validation that the window length is a multiple of 3 and the codon count matches the residue range.

Batch a whole sequencing plate: iterate a variant table of (ab1 file, start, end, reverse_complement, aa_anno_range, label) and write <variant>_nt_logo.pdf plus <variant>_aa_logo.pdf and an AA-proportion CSV per sample.

Join the sequencing facility's QC .xls (columns TrackingNumber, DNAType, TubeLabel, DNAName, PrimerName, TemplateName, QualitySCore, CRL, QV20Plus) so low-quality reads are flagged before anyone reads an editing percentage off a noisy trace.

Parse a FlowJo-exported gate statistics .xls (columns Depth, Name, Statistic, #Cells, where Name is the full slash-delimited gate path) into a tidy per-sample DataFrame, selecting only real sample specimens and skipping single-stain compensation controls.
Chain parent-relative FlowJo percentages into a percentage of a chosen ancestor gate (the LSK-of-single-cells case: Q2% x Lin-% / 100), which is the step most often done wrong by hand.
Convert frequencies into absolute cell counts from viability x volume x concentration and report fold expansion against an input count.

Draw the three validated flow panels: grouped bar of counts with K/M tick formatting, linear stacked composition bar with in-segment percentage labels, and log-space stacked bar where each segment's height is log10(total) x fraction with 10^n tick labels.
designs.inputs: SANGER: a folder of ABI .ab1 files (the facility ships e.g. MEC_KP_PK_Genotyping_30-1331125458_ab1/ with names like KP_Sort-p53_F.ab1, 5_R248Q_FW_N-P2_FW.ab1, plus a parallel *_seq/ folder of .seq FASTA that this skill does NOT need). Per sample the user must supply the window to plot: 1-based inclusive start and end coordinates in the AB1-called sequence (PBAS1, i.e. what SnapGene/Benchling shows for that read, NOT genomic coordinates), whether the read is on the reverse strand (reverse_complement=True for an _R/_RV primer read of a plus-strand gene), and optionally aa_anno_range=(first_aa,last_aa) for residue numbering. Window length must be a multiple of 3 and in frame for 'aa'. Recommended input format: a small CSV variant table with columns ab1, variant, start, end, reverse_complement, aa_first, aa_last. Optional: the facility QC workbook (30-*_QSCRL.xls) for QualitySCore/CRL/QV20Plus. No reference genome or $LAB_DATA_ROOT lookup is needed for the Sanger path; if the user instead gives a genomic/transcript coordinate, the window must first be located in the read (align the .seq/PBAS1 against the expected amplicon) — the source code does not do this and the skill must ask for read coordinates rather than guess. FLOW: a FlowJo "export group statistics" .xls (legacy BIFF .xls, columns Depth / Name / Statistic / #Cells; Name is the full gate path like Specimen_001_Sample 1.fcs/Lymphocytes/Single Cells/Q2: APC-A+ , BV421-A+/Lin-/CD150+), the list of sample specimen names to include, the gate paths of interest, and for absolute counts the input cell number, final viability, volume and cells/mL. Raw .fcs files are not supported.
designs.outputs: SANGER: per variant a nucleotide logo PDF (<variant>_nt_logo.pdf) and an amino-acid logo PDF (<variant>_aa_logo.pdf) with editable text (pdf.fonttype 42), the per-position nucleotide proportion table and the per-residue amino-acid proportion DataFrame/CSV (the numeric editing readout: e.g. fraction Q vs R at residue 248, and any bystander amino acid at a neighboring codon), plus an optional QC table merging QualitySCore/CRL/QV20Plus per read and a one-line call per sample (edited fraction at the target residue, WT fraction, bystanders above a threshold). FLOW: flow_summary.csv (one row per sample, with both % and #Cells for each requested gate plus the chained percent-of-ancestor column), printed absolute counts and fold expansion, and the three PDFs flow_bar_plot.pdf, flow_stacked_linear.pdf, flow_stacked_log.pdf.
designs.envDependencies: Runs in a plain analysis environment, NOT pegg_env — no scikit-learn/pickle constraint applies here, so do not couple it to the pegg pin (Python 3.9/3.10 + scikit-learn==1.1.1 + numpy<2 is required only for skills that call pegg's scoring models). `start` and `end` are 1-based inclusive coordinates in the AB1's own called sequence (PBAS1), NOT genomic, transcript or amplicon coordinates. The code does `range(start-1, end)` with no alignment step and no bounds check — an out-of-range end raises an opaque IndexError from `positions[idx]`, and a window that is merely shifted by a few bases silently produces a plausible-looking logo of the wrong codons. Always print the called bases in the window and confirm they match the expected amplicon before trusting the proportions.

For 'aa' logos the window must be in frame AND a multiple of 3. The code validates the multiple-of-3 and the codon-count-vs-aa_anno_range, but it CANNOT detect a frame shift — a window offset by 1 nt yields a full amino-acid logo that is entirely wrong. Verify by checking that the WT residue identity at each labelled position matches the known protein sequence (e.g. R at 248, R at 273).

Reverse-complement is only correct if it is applied to the right read. A reverse-primer read (_R, _RV, *_RV.ab1) of a plus-strand gene needs reverse_complement=True; the notebook's own blocks are inconsistent (R273C/R273H/R280G/R245Q/L249P/R277G reverse reads are plotted with reverse_complement=False, while the forward reads for R248Q/R270C/R270H use True) because what matters is the orientation of the read relative to the coding strand, not the primer name. Determine orientation by comparing the read's called sequence to the expected coding sequence, not by the filename.

Trace channel mapping depends on the instrument: `channel_data = {b: abif[f'DATA{i+9}'] for i,b in enumerate(abif['FWO_1'].decode())}`. FWO_1 is b'GATC' on these files, so DATA9=G, DATA10=A, DATA11=T, DATA12=C — do NOT assume alphabetical ACGT order or hardcode DATA9..12 to A,C,G,T. Also use DATA9-12 (the analyzed/smoothed traces), not DATA1-4 (raw).

Proportions are peak-height ratios at the called peak, which are a proxy for allele fraction, not a calibrated measurement. They are biased by dye mobility, signal saturation, nearby indels and low CRL; the facility QC columns QualitySCore, CRL and QV20Plus (in 30-*_QSCRL.xls) should be checked, and an indel-containing edit makes the trace downstream of the edit uninterpretable entirely. Report these as approximate editing fractions and never as an exact allele frequency without an orthogonal amplicon-NGS/CRISPResso2 readout (that is the ngs-screen skill).

The AA collapse assumes the three positions of a codon are statistically independent, which is false for a real edited pool: a cell carrying the edit usually carries all of its bystanders together. For a multi-nucleotide edit the product-of-marginals AA proportions are only an approximation and can show haplotypes that do not exist. Say this when the window contains more than one edited base.

FlowJo statistics are percent-of-PARENT, not percent-of-total. The notebook's `lsk_of_sc = (q2_pct/100)*(lsk_pct/100)*100` exists for exactly this reason, and skipping that chaining is the most common error in flow readouts. Anything two or more gates deep must be chained through every intermediate gate.

`get(path)` matches the FULL slash-delimited gate path by exact string equality after .strip(), and returns (nan, 0) silently when nothing matches — a renamed gate, an extra space, or FlowJo's exact quadrant naming ('Q2: APC-A+ , BV421-A+' has a space before the comma) produces NaN columns and a plot of nothing rather than an error. List the available gate paths first and make the lookup raise.

The flow export contains single-stain compensation controls as separate specimens (Specimen_001_APC.fcs, _BV421.fcs, _BV510.fcs, _PE.fcs, _PEcy7.fcs) alongside the real samples (Specimen_001_Sample 1/2/3.fcs). The notebook hardcodes samples = ['Sample 1','Sample 2','Sample 3'] for that reason. Never glob all specimens — the controls have near-zero LSK and would silently dilute every mean.

Deep gates here have tiny denominators: Sample 1's LSK CD150+ CD34- gate is 4 cells of 260 LSK. Percentages off single-digit cell counts are noise; the parser should carry the #Cells column alongside every % so the skill can refuse to plot or can annotate n, and `final_total_live = 0.452*3*12*1e6` (viability x volume(mL) x cells/mL) plus `initial_LSK = 24_000` are hand-entered hemocytometer/counter numbers that must become named arguments, not literals.

The log-space stacked bar is a presentational construction, not a log axis: each segment's height is `log10(total) * (count/total)`, so segment heights are proportional to composition while the bar's total height reads as log10(count). Segment boundaries do NOT correspond to their counts on the 10^n tick labels. Keep the two-panel linear+log pair the notebook produced and label the log one carefully, or a reader will misread segment sizes.
